newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan may face debt repayment crunch in June.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan may face debt repayment crunch in June.

text.p: Pakistan will meet debt repayments scheduled for April-May, but later months could prove difficult, a research report said on Friday.

"April and May are relatively lean months for debt servicing repayments -- with approximately $250 million falling due each month," the report issued by brokerage house Khadim Ali Shah Bukhari & Co (KASB) said.
"The June-July period, however, could prove to be the crunch time."

The report said Pakistan faced expected repayments of $600 million in June and July. At the same time, foreign reserves would be under pressure due to higher imports after a 10 percent regulatory duty on imports is abolished on July 1.
Pakistani importers are holding back because of the reduction in tariffs to 45 percent from 65 percent and abolition of 10 percent regulatory duty on imports effective from July 1, the report said.
"The trade balance in the next three months should be lower because traders would hold back on imports in light of tariff cuts from July 1," the report added.
The State (central) Bank of Pakistan (SBP) said on Friday that cash foreign exchange reserves slipped to $945 million in March from $1.0 billion in February.
The report said around $300 million to $400 million placed with the SBP in high yield special accounts would be maturing in June putting more pressure on the reserves.
Raza Mirza, head of research at KASB, said creditors would face a dilemma of how to get back, and out, with their dollars and at the same time not trigger a default.
The deposits were made under a scheme launched by the SBP on October 22, 1996, offering 17 percent annual return on the rupee equivalent of foreign currency deposits brought by banks from abroad.
KASB said Pakistan's reserves needed to be increased to more than $2 billion through non-interest bearing resources, primarily privatisation of state assets and an increase in exports.
Pakistan plans to privatise state-run units and use the money for debt repayments.
